planting.note: Plant divisions or container plugs in spring directly into thin, gravelly, calcium-rich soil pockets in full sun to light shade; Richardson's sedge is a signature species of Great Lakes alvar pavement and needs the sharp drainage of a crushed-limestone or gravel bed rather than a typical garden loam.

directions: Richardson's sedge forms low, dense tufts of narrow, slightly curled, blue-green leaves and sends up short flowering stalks tipped with dark purplish-brown spikes in very early spring, well before most other sedges. It is one of the characteristic plants of Great Lakes limestone alvar pavement, where thin soil pockets over bedrock drain quickly and bake hot in summer yet freeze hard in winter, conditions this species tolerates without complaint. In the garden it works best as an edging or crevice plant in a lean, rocky, alkaline bed rather than ordinary border soil, where richer, moisture-retentive conditions tend to favor coarser competing grasses over it. Established clumps spread slowly and can be divided in spring to extend a planting.

planting.note: Plant small divisions or plugs in spring into shallow, lean, alkaline, gritty soil in full sun; this diminutive fleabane needs the open, uncompeted conditions of a rock garden or trough rather than a typical perennial bed, where larger neighbors quickly crowd it out.

directions: Hyssop-leaved fleabane forms a tight, spreading mat of narrow, dark green leaves studded in summer with small, white-rayed, yellow-centered daisies carried just above the foliage on wiry stems. It occurs as a disjunct calciphile on Great Lakes alvar pavement and limestone shorelines, far south of its main circumboreal range across northern Canada and the Rockies, rooting directly into cracks and thin gravel over bedrock. Its tolerance for shallow, mineral-poor, droughty soil and its tidy mat-forming habit make it a good fit for crevice gardens, troughs, and alpine-style rockeries rather than conventional borders. Shear lightly after bloom to keep the mat dense and encourage repeat flowering into fall.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into calcareous, gravelly to loamy soil that stays damp in the seasonally wet swales of an alvar or fen planting; unlike most dry-pavement alvar sedges, Crawe's sedge wants steady moisture around its roots and does not tolerate prolonged summer drought.

directions: Crawe's sedge grows as loose tufts of glossy, yellow-green, grass-like leaves topped by slender stalks bearing a single terminal male spike above shorter female spikes in late spring. It inhabits the shallow, seasonally flooded swales, pavement depressions, and marly fen edges found within Great Lakes alvar landscapes, places that stay saturated in spring and early summer even as the surrounding bare rock bakes dry. In cultivation it suits the damp margins of a rain garden, pond edge, or constructed fen bed built over limestone gravel, rather than a dry rock garden setting. It spreads gradually by short rhizomes and can be divided every few years to propagate new clumps.

planting.note: Cold-stratify seed over winter and start indoors, or set out nursery-grown plugs in spring, into shallow, calcareous, gritty soil that holds spring moisture in a rock garden pocket or trough; this tiny primrose needs reliable moisture while in growth but will rot if left standing in water.

directions: Bird's-eye primrose sends up a small basal rosette of spoon-shaped leaves with a mealy white coating on the underside, and in mid to late spring produces short stalks topped by clusters of small, pink to lavender flowers with a bright yellow eye. It is famous from the limestone alvar pavement and cobble shorelines of the Bruce Peninsula, Door County, and other Great Lakes sites, where it roots into damp seams and depressions that stay moist from spring seepage even as the surrounding rock dries by midsummer. Because it is small and short-rooted, it is best grown in a rock garden trough or crevice bed with constant light moisture rather than a typical dry alpine scree. Division of offsets after flowering is the most reliable way to increase an established planting.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into lean, well-drained, calcareous soil alongside established native grasses and forbs; bastard toadflax is a facultative root hemiparasite that grows and spreads far more vigorously with host plant roots nearby than when sown by itself in bare ground.

directions: Bastard toadflax is an understated, blue-green-leaved perennial that forms loose colonies by spreading underground rhizomes and sends up clusters of small, star-shaped white flowers in late spring, followed by a single round, bronze, berry-like fruit per stem. It thrives on the thin, dry, calcium-rich soils of Great Lakes alvar openings and dry prairies, where it taps into the roots of neighboring grasses and forbs through haustoria for part of its water and nutrients without being strictly dependent on any one host. Unlike obligate parasites such as Indian paintbrush, it can be established from seed sown among existing native vegetation and will spread on its own over time once settled. Site it in an open, low-competition native planting rather than a conventional mulched border, where its subtle color and texture are easily lost among showier perennials.

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring into damp, calcareous, gravelly to mucky soil in full sun; slender reedgrass belongs to the wet swales and fen edges of alvar landscapes, so site it in a rain garden or pond-margin bed rather than a dry rock planting.

directions: Slender reedgrass is a fine-textured, cool-season bunchgrass with narrow, upright blue-green leaves and slim, purplish-green flowering panicles that rise above the foliage in early summer and fade to tan by fall. It grows in the seasonally saturated swales, marly fens, and wet pavement depressions scattered through Great Lakes alvar landscapes, as well as in northern wet meadows and shorelines beyond the alvar zone. Its narrow, upright habit and tolerance for calcareous, periodically flooded soil make it a useful, lower-profile alternative to larger reed grasses in a constructed fen, rain garden, or restoration planting. Clumps increase slowly and can be divided in spring to fill out a planting.
